title: Navigation and Cross-Country Flight Planning
summary: Build a route you can explain, a fuel plan that survives change, and a way to recognize when the real flight stops matching the plan.
objectives: Separate course, heading, and track, and apply wind, variation, and compass corrections.
Develop a route, altitude, time, and fuel plan from current information and aircraft performance.
Update the plan in flight, divert early, and use appropriate assistance if position or conditions become uncertain.

sections.title: Course is the plan; heading is a control input
sections.body:
Course is the intended path over the ground. Heading is where the aircraft’s longitudinal axis points. Track is the path actually made over the ground. Wind makes those three directions differ. True airspeed describes motion through the air; groundspeed describes motion across the surface.

The airspeed vector and wind vector add to form the groundspeed vector. A crosswind calls for a heading correction into the wind to hold the intended course. A headwind mainly reduces groundspeed, increasing time and fuel for the same distance.

Apply it: establish whether a reported wind direction is “from” and whether the source uses true or magnetic reference. E6B or EFB planning should convert the reported wind into a consistent reference frame before solving the wind triangle. A plausible-looking heading can still be wrong if the references were mixed.
sections.deep:
For a pure 20 kt crosswind and 100 kt true airspeed, holding the desired track requires an into-wind correction of arcsin(20/100), approximately 11.5°. Some of the airspeed vector now cancels crosswind; the along-track groundspeed is approximately √(100² − 20²) = 98 kt. Crab angle is therefore not created by simply subtracting the wind speed from true airspeed.

For basic navigation calculations, apply wind to true course to get true heading, then variation to get magnetic heading, then the aircraft’s compass-deviation correction when using the magnetic compass. Check the signs with a sketch or trusted method. A GPS track display helps assess drift but does not eliminate the need to understand the desired ground path.

sections.title: Choose checkpoints that can prove your position
sections.body:
Use current sectional or terminal charts and applicable airport information to build a route around terrain, obstacles, controlled airspace, special-use activity, and practical landing options. A straight line is only the first candidate route.

Good visual checkpoints are distinctive, easy to identify from the expected direction, and spaced so a wrong position can be detected early. A uniquely shaped lake, a recognizable road-river crossing, or an airport can work better than a similar-looking town. Choose spacing to match speed, visibility, terrain, and workload; “every 10–15 NM” is a planning suggestion rather than a regulation.

Read airport elevation, runway information, obstacles, and chart annotations with the correct units and altitude references. A maximum elevation figure is an area summary, not a route-specific clearance, an IFR minimum altitude, or a guarantee of legal terrain separation.
sections.deep:
Pilotage identifies position from observed landmarks. Dead reckoning predicts position from heading, groundspeed, and elapsed time. Used together, they expose errors: if the expected landmark does not appear when predicted, either the position, speed, wind, identification, or timing assumption needs review.

Charts also simplify information. A landmark can be obscured, a tower can be added between editions, and an EFB layer can be turned off. Review the legend, effective dates, NOTAMs, and terrain along plausible escape routes. Download the needed charts before flight and know which information will remain available after loss of internet, power, or a location signal.

sections.title: Build the time and fuel calculation leg by leg
sections.body:
For each leg, identify distance and true course, obtain an appropriate wind forecast, use the aircraft’s expected true airspeed and fuel flow, and calculate heading, groundspeed, time, and fuel. Include climb, cruise, descent, taxi, and other relevant fuel use with the performance data applicable to those phases.

Time in minutes equals distance in NM divided by groundspeed in knots, multiplied by 60. Fuel for a phase equals its duration in hours multiplied by the appropriate fuel-flow rate. Keep units visible. A 60 NM leg at 90 kt takes 40 minutes, not one hour; at 9 gal/hr, that cruise segment uses 6 gal.

Apply it: make a nav log that the pilot can actually use. Record expected checkpoint times and fuel states, then compare them with the flight rather than treating the finished worksheet as an administrative exercise.
sections.deep:
An EFB automates arithmetic, not truth. Aircraft identity, usable fuel, loading, power setting, fuel flow, departure time, altitude, and wind data all influence the output. A default performance profile can turn optimistic inputs into highly precise-looking errors. Verify representative results against the POH and observed aircraft performance.

In flight, recompute groundspeed from a known distance and elapsed time. If 30 NM took 24 minutes, groundspeed was 75 kt. A forecast 90 kt groundspeed for the next 60 NM would predict 40 minutes; continuing at 75 kt would take 48 minutes. This is why unexpected headwind must change fuel and diversion decisions before the reserve becomes small.

sections.title: Choose an altitude for the whole route
sections.body:
Altitude selection must satisfy terrain and obstacle clearance, airspace, weather, aircraft climb capability, navigation coverage, pilot limits, and fuel efficiency. A favorable wind is useful only if the airplane can reach and safely use that altitude.

Under the ordinary § 91.159 rule, VFR level cruising flight more than 3,000 ft above the surface uses the magnetic course: 000°–179° calls for odd thousands plus 500 ft MSL, and 180°–359° calls for even thousands plus 500 ft MSL below 18,000 ft MSL. The regulation contains exceptions and ATC authorization provisions. Do not select the side of the rule from heading or GPS true track.

Apply it: a wind-corrected heading of 175° does not control the rule when the magnetic course is 185°. The course points to the even-thousand-plus-500 side.
sections.deep:
The height trigger uses the surface below you; the selected cruising altitude uses MSL. Over rising terrain, one constant MSL altitude can move closer to the ground. Reassess terrain clearance and the applicability of the cruising-altitude rule along the route rather than only at departure.

Plan descent as deliberately as climb. The common 3 NM per 1,000 ft descent estimate describes an approximate geometric path, not a guaranteed descent performance or a universal procedure. Required vertical speed depends on groundspeed, desired path, configuration, and aircraft limits. Begin early enough to manage airspace, temperatures, airspeed, traffic, and arrival workload without a rushed descent.

sections.title: Legal reserve is the floor of the plan
sections.body:
For a VFR airplane flight, § 91.151 requires enough fuel at departure, considering wind and forecast weather, to reach the first intended landing point and then continue at normal cruising speed for at least 30 minutes by day or 45 minutes at night. Use usable fuel, not the total capacity printed on a tank placard.

The legal planning minimum is not a target for how little fuel should remain at landing. Add the fuel needed for realistic delays, climb, diversions, weather uncertainty, and the operator’s or pilot’s chosen reserve. Establish an early decision point for an unplanned fuel stop.

Worked example: for an illustrative constant 10 gal/hr flight lasting 90 minutes, with no additional taxi fuel in this simplified calculation, the trip uses 15 gal. Adding the daytime 30-minute reserve adds 5 gal, giving a 20 gal regulatory planning baseline.
sections.deep:
A percentage contingency and a time reserve solve different problems. Ten percent extra cruise fuel may be only a few minutes on a short trip, while a long headwind leg can consume a large amount of fuel before the error is recognized. Express the actual fuel state both as gallons and as remaining time at a defensible flow rate.

Fuel exhaustion means the usable supply has been depleted. Fuel starvation means fuel is not reaching the engine despite fuel remaining somewhere in the aircraft. Tank selection, imbalance, venting, pumps, and aircraft procedures matter. A large calculated reserve cannot protect against an incorrectly selected tank or an inaccurate starting-fuel assumption.

sections.title: Brief the weather and preserve a usable alternative
sections.body:
Preflight information must support the proposed operation. Review current and forecast weather, NOTAMs, TFRs, airport conditions, delays, runway lengths, available alternatives, and aircraft performance. Use § 91.103 to understand the applicable preflight duty rather than treating a mnemonic as the entire rule.

Ask what will make the plan unacceptable, when that change can be recognized, and where to land if it occurs. Set limits before departure, when there is time to think clearly. A usable alternative must fit weather, fuel, runway, terrain, opening hours, and the aircraft’s equipment.

A VFR flight plan supports search-and-rescue processes. It does not provide an ATC clearance or automatically start flight following. Arrange activation and closure by an appropriate available method, and update the plan when the route or destination changes.
sections.deep:
Separate a forecast from an observation and compare both with trends. A departure airport reporting good conditions does not establish the route, pass, or destination will remain suitable at arrival. Consider ceilings, visibility, winds, convection, icing exposure, density altitude, and daylight relevant to the actual flight.

External pressure can make an unsafe plan look attractive: an instructor appointment, passengers, a return commitment, or the desire to finish a cross-country requirement. Build alternatives that remove that pressure, such as a different day, a fuel stop, a shorter route, or ground transport. A briefing is a continuing assessment; use updated information in flight when available.

sections.title: Divert early; ask for help before uncertainty grows
sections.body:
When the planned destination or route becomes unsuitable, select a realistic alternative while there is still time and fuel. Establish a safe heading, estimate distance and groundspeed, calculate time and fuel, assess terrain and airspace, obtain airport and weather information, and refine the plan as workload permits.

If position is uncertain, keep aircraft control first. Use reliable landmarks, a second navigation source, or ATC/Flight Service assistance. A climb may improve visibility or radio reception only when weather, terrain, airspace, and aircraft performance permit it. A memorized “climb” step is not authority to enter cloud or violate an airspace boundary.

Apply it: communicate the actual problem plainly. If the situation is urgent, use appropriate urgency or distress language rather than delaying help to avoid embarrassment. Declare an emergency when warranted.
sections.deep:
A good diversion estimate is intentionally coarse at first. At 90 kt groundspeed, 15 NM takes about 10 minutes; at a 9 gal/hr flow, that segment consumes about 1.5 gal before approach and other allowances. A quick estimate identifies whether an option is plausible while a detailed calculation can follow.

The trap is persisting with a detailed electronic setup while the airplane flies farther from the safe option. Reduce workload, share tasks appropriately, and maintain a visual flight path. If a navigation aid or EFB disagrees with the outside scene, do not force the scene to match the display. Re-establish the aircraft’s position from dependable information before continuing into more demanding terrain or airspace.

teachBack: Use a wind triangle to explain why heading and track can differ while the aircraft remains on course.
Build one leg of a nav log and state which inputs would change time and fuel most.
Explain why the VFR cruising-altitude rule uses magnetic course and a height-above-surface trigger.
Give a diversion plan for worsening weather that includes a fuel and terrain check.
takeaways: A useful plan predicts checkpoints and fuel states that can be checked during flight.
Use magnetic course for the ordinary VFR cruising-altitude rule, not wind-corrected heading.
Preserve time, fuel, and alternatives; early changes are easier than late recoveries.

quiz.question: A VFR airplane is in level cruising flight more than 3,000 ft above the surface, below 18,000 ft MSL, with no ATC exception. Magnetic course is 185°, while wind-corrected heading is 175°. Which cruising altitude fits the direction rule?
feedback: 5,500 ft belongs to the 000°–179° magnetic-course side, which is not this course.
185° magnetic course uses even thousands plus 500 ft, so 6,500 ft fits the direction rule.
An ordinary 6,000 ft altitude is not an even-thousand-plus-500 VFR cruising altitude.
7,500 ft belongs to the opposite magnetic-course side.
quiz.hint: The rule names course, not heading.

quiz.question: A known 60 NM cruise leg is planned at 90 kt groundspeed and 9 gal/hr. Ignoring climb and other phases, what are its time and fuel?
feedback: At 90 kt, the airplane covers 60 NM in two thirds of an hour, not one hour.
Two thirds of an hour at 9 gal/hr uses 6 gal.
60/90 hour equals 40 minutes; 9 × 2/3 equals 6 gal.
90 minutes at this speed would cover 135 NM, not 60 NM.
quiz.hint: Convert the leg duration to hours before multiplying by gallons per hour.

quiz.question: For a simplified daytime VFR airplane flight, the first intended landing is 90 minutes away. Assume 10 gal/hr throughout and no additional taxi fuel. What is the § 91.151 trip-plus-reserve baseline?
feedback: 15 gal covers the 90-minute trip but omits the daytime reserve.
2.5 gal adds only 15 minutes at this flow rate.
22.5 gal represents a 45-minute reserve, the airplane night minimum in this simplified scenario.
The trip needs 15 gal and the 30-minute reserve needs 5 gal, totaling 20 gal.
quiz.hint: Add the daytime reserve duration to the trip before converting to fuel.

quiz.question: What is the primary role of an ordinary VFR flight plan?
options: Support search and rescue if the flight becomes overdue
Authorize entry into Class B airspace
Guarantee that the destination weather will remain VFR
feedback: The plan supports overdue-aircraft and search-and-rescue processes when properly handled.
Class B entry still needs a separate explicit ATC clearance.
Advisory service must be established separately; filing a VFR plan does not create it.
A flight plan is not a forecast guarantee.
quiz.hint: Distinguish a filed record from a live ATC service.

quiz.question: A student becomes uncertain of position under a low overcast near controlled airspace. How should “climb” in a lost-procedure mnemonic be interpreted?
options: Climb into the overcast to improve radio coverage
Consider a climb only if weather, terrain, airspace, and performance permit it
Climb above the Class B shelf without contacting ATC
Always climb before asking ATC for help
feedback: A mnemonic does not authorize an unqualified VFR pilot to enter cloud.
Climbing is conditional; safe aircraft control and early assistance remain priorities.
The maneuver must still respect airspace entry and equipment requirements.
Help can be requested immediately; a climb is not a prerequisite.
quiz.hint: The mnemonic does not override the conditions outside the aircraft.

quiz.question: An EFB predicts a fast, fuel-efficient trip using a default aircraft profile. What should the pilot do before accepting it?
options: Assume precision in the output proves the profile is accurate
Replace all POH planning with the EFB estimate
Verify loading, usable fuel, performance profile, departure time, winds, and route assumptions
Use the result if another airplane of the same model flew it last week
feedback: Precise arithmetic can still operate on inaccurate inputs.
The EFB is a calculation tool whose aircraft performance assumptions need verification.
The forecast depends on those inputs and should be checked against applicable aircraft data and conditions.
Aircraft condition, loading, weather, and installed equipment can differ.
quiz.hint: Ask which assumptions generated the output.
